utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Diarra this morning won't be able to be with us. So in accordance with Rule 15 bis, the remaining Judges decided, that it is in the interests of justice, for us to continue the procedures. It is so decided. Mr. Krsnik, we have received your filings concerning with the videolink witnesses and there are some questions I would like to ask you, if we could go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And could we have the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please sit down. Did you have a good rest last night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone and speak up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yesterday it was extremely hot in The Hague. Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness MM?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nods. But could the witness please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness could you please move closer to the microphone or move the microphone a bit closer to you? Witness, yesterday we left off talking about the 17th of September, and I have a few more questions to ask about this day. You were talking about soldiers from Livno who were crossing the Bulevar on the left side of the area where the Vinko Skrobo was responsible for; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, how did you know that these soldiers who were there were soldiers from Livno?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody knew who came from where, whose turn it would be to hold the line, whose shifts would be because that did not change. I mean the units that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So is it correct then that these soldiers from Livno were also permanently stationed at that part of the Bulevar or was that a group of soldiers just coming in for that particular operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps they would take shifts a month or two later. And then another unit would come. But as a rule, it was always the same ones -- I mean the same unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you've also testified that some of these soldiers, when they were crossing the Bulevar, got injured and killed on that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the Livno unit, them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, since the Vinko Skrobo unit was very close by, did any of the soldiers of the Vinko Skrobo unit assist in getting the bodies from the Bulevar back to -- well, let's say West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because we had our area and that was our responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So on that day you never saw any of these soldiers and you never assisted in any way this group of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this group from Livno?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When the action ended, when it was foiled, it was only then that we learned what had happened to those people, from stories. We could not see them personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Witness, you testified in direct examination that there was one occasion where you helped a woman and two children to cross the Bulevar. Were these Muslims? Were these people Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall the date when this crossover took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date. It was a long time ago. So that the exact date, not even a month, I could not really say, had it happened four, five, maybe seven years ago, I would have remembered probably but after all this time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, did it happen more often that Muslims would make individual arrangements with soldiers at the confrontation line to get over the confrontation line or was your case an exceptional case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, these were exceptions at the request, at the insistence, please, to be taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did Muslims ever pay -- offered money to soldiers to get them across the line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, did you ever see at around the health centre, did you ever see a large group of Muslims crossing the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know whether soldiers of the ATG Vinko Skrobo were ever involved in the forcible transfer of Muslims from West Mostar to East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P456.1, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, this exhibit is a report from the military police and I'd like you to read the paragraph under zone number 3. And I'm especially interested in the second paragraph of that chapter. Now, witness, this reports talks about the expulsion of Muslims on the 13th and 14th of June, 1993, from an area in Mostar called Dum. And the expulsion was done by Stela with a group of around 40 well-armed soldiers. Now, you've testified that in early June, when you joined the ATG Mrmak, the unit counted about 40 soldiers. Were you present on this occasion which is described in this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I'm not aware of this happening, because if there were 40 odd men there, then who manned the line? The health centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that on the 13th and 14th of June, you were at the confrontation line at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I don't know if I was there on that date but at that time, the front line by the health centre was already being held. Now, I can't remember shifts and dates. It was -- I can't even remember years let alone dates or days when I was somewhere because one had to work every day. I mean it to hold the line, to be on the reserve, rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I have one more documents which I want to you look at which is Exhibit P599.1. Witness, this is an official note from the military police dated the 14th September, 1993, I'd like you to read this note, please. Now, witness, this note talks about the expulsion of Muslims by the ATG Mrmak and the ATG Benko Penavic on the 11th, 12th and 13th of September, in an area at the Omladinska Street and the XVIth Street, in Roman figures. Do you know where that area is in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know it because I live there, I lived in that town, and it is all in the west part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, maybe if the witness could be given the map Exhibit D2/37, and maybe in private session he could mark on the map where this area actually is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And these instances where you saw that apartments were looted, was this all in the area where you lived or was this other areas as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: It usually happened in the area where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you ever get a chance to see who actually did loot these apartments? Were these soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were both, both soldiers and civilians. There were usually all people who were not from Mostar, people who had moved in because there was a large number of refugees and that is why they were all these expulsions and people tried to manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination? Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few brief questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown this photograph that we saw yesterday an old picture of the health centre P14.20?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Witness, will you look at this photograph that you saw yesterday and in answer to a question from the Prosecution, when the 17th of September was discussed, that on this photograph, in this area, a tank did not appear. Could the photograph be placed on the ELMO, please? So is it true that you said yesterday that the tank was not to be seen in this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, because I was here in the bunker, in this part of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: My question is: Why the tank didn't appear here because it didn't come there at all or is it because you can't see the spot that he reached, it never got there, or is it that this photograph doesn't show that spot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tank didn't come there at all, because the hedgehogs had not been removed nor the antitank mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can the spot be seen on this photograph where the tank stopped or is that spot not visible on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That spot cannot be seen on this photograph because the tank never got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Fine. Yesterday, during the direct examination, you mentioned the name of a soldier known as Svabo. Was that Svabo a foreigner, a foreign national?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but he was engaged in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: It tell me, please, were there other foreigners engaged in HVO units and specifically in the Skrobo unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there have been one or two of them, but they only spent a few days there and then they would disappear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Were they paid? Did they receive a salary? Did they work for money as soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that because I don't know, but I do know that they also wore HVO uniforms and insignia. Now, whether they were paid, who paid them and how much, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Just one more question. Did Vinko Martinovic, Stela, come to the front line regularly or did he spend his time in the base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: He spent most of his time in the base, like any commander he would come to visit us, not every day but at least once or twice a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Clark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. I have some questions arising out of those last questions which Mr. Par put to you about the base. Was it part of your duty to serve time at the base from time to time or were you always at the front line when you were on duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our working day or our shift lasted 12 hours. Then our duty was to spend all 12 hours on the front line. In the rear, in the third building, which was all part of the health centre, we would organise shifts so that some people would be at the bunker and others would rest so we rotated. At the end of our shift, we would go to the base, report there as to how things had evolved, and then we would go home, except in exceptional cases when a report may have been received of an imminent attack, then a certain number of people would be on the ready or on the alert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So can I take it from your answer that when you were on duty, the only time you would be at the base was to furnish a report on your way home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the end of the shift, like a briefing. We would go there to brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And when you went to the base for briefing or debriefing, generally how many of Mr. Martinovic's soldiers would be at the base? In other words what I really want to know is were there soldiers who were permanently allocated to duties at the base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was just the logistics that was with him there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You may not know the answer to this, Mr. MM, but if Mr. Martinovic needed to go and sort out a problem, away from the base and away from the front line, and he was taking his -- some of his men with him, where would those men come from? Would they be logistics or would they be reserves or do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I don't know what to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: If you don't know, that's the best answer. How did you receive your meals, if you were on duty? Did you receive a meal as part of your remuneration?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did receive meals. As at home, in our restaurant, which was nearby, near the base, we had breakfast, lunch and dinner. People who had no one at home, who were alone, whose families were not at home, then they would get their meals there. As for the soldiers, when going on duty for their shift, they could eat on the way there or returning from the shift, and during the night, we would get a lunch packet as an additional meal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the restaurant that you had breakfast, lunch and dinner at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's called Hladovina even now. Hladovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Are you sure about that evidence, that you had three meals a day there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whenever anyone was hungry, he could -- he would go and eat. So there wasn't any food in between meals. So either on the way to your shift or when you finish your shift.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday during the course of your evidence through Mr. Par, that from time to time, prisoners were brought over to the health centre, if there was a job to be done and they were in what you called the alcoholic's club, I think you called it, and I think you described that they were mostly making coffee or cleaning up or repairing something that needed to be repaired, and you also described how it was necessary for a request to be put in and for paper work to be carried out before Vinko Skrobo unit could receive a prisoner. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question. The requests were sent to the defence of the town and they would permit a certain number of men to come that were needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. MM, that's exactly my recollection of what you said. I was just wondering how you would be familiar with that procedure. How would you know that, as you on many occasions have told us you were merely a foot soldier and you didn't know what was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply I communicated with everyone, with the prisoners, and with the soldiers. I would ask the prisoners how they felt, were they afraid, did they need anything, that they shouldn't be afraid, that nobody would do anything to them there, because I myself was a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: On the day of the abortive tank attack, I think we could describe it as that, do you remember if a soldier from your unit who had a nickname Brada was there? Do you have any recollection of his being there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all had to be there, I think all of us were there, the whole unit was on the front line. Now, perhaps I can remember some ten or so men from my group, because we were right next to one another. As for the operation itself, it's absurd to expect people to look around and see where everyone was. All you care about is to remain alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I can accept that. I'm sure it was a fairly terrifying experience that day. Do you have any recollection of a Danish soldier being there that day? It may well be he wasn't in your little group but do you have any recollection of a Danish soldier being there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I don't know anything about a Danish man. It's the first I hear of a Danish man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you remember a Danish man or even two being members of the Vinko Skrobo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything with certainty. I can only assert things about the group I was in, and the men who were around me in the group. We were all Croats and we were all from the town and there were no foreigners in that group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did you have a card, an identity card, which indicated that you were a member of Vinko Skrobo, with your photograph on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had HVO cards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And was it an identity card with a photograph on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received five or six such ID cards, and I mean throughout the duration of the war, because these changed and there was a photograph on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did they change according to the particular unit you were attached to? Is that why you had so many of them because you changed units several times, or your units developed into different units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I changed two or three units for the whole duration of the war, three actually, but for the last three years, I received three different ID cards with photographs. Now, why this procedure, why they changed it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And during the period that you were with Mr. Martinovic's unit in 1993, did any of your identity cards indicate that you were part of the Convicts Battalion? I ask you that, Mr. MM, because we've seen Mr. Martinovic's identity card, which he himself handed up to the Court through his counsel.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's unclear to me now that you mention the Convicts Battalion, because we were not members of the Convicts. We were an independent, anti-terrorist unit, ATG Vinko Skrobo, belonging to the town. So we belonged to the city HVO. All the units that were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The question I asked you was: Did you have a card, an identity card from the HVO during the period that you were with Mr. Martinovic's unit in 1993, indicating that you -- that the unit was part of the Convicts Battalion. I'm not saying whether it's correct or not, but did you have a card that said that were you a member of the Convicts Battalion during that period, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim with certainty. I have all the ID's at home but I think I received such an ID card. Now, what it says, I don't know, because before that, I had an ID card of the 4th Battalion that I was in. I think I received that ID card. That applied for the Guards Brigade later on as well. Because one -- they would get lost and then they would be distributed quite easily and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Is what you're saying Mr. MM is that you can't exclude the possibility that your 1993 card might have indicated the word "Convicts Battalion," but you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not a member of the Convicts Battalion under any circumstances. I cannot claim that that is what it says there. I think it says, "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna HVO."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges' questions? Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Just one question. Witness, when discussing the procedure for bringing prisoners of war, the request to had to be approved and so on, were you referring to prisoners being brought from Heliodrom or from the base to the health centre, for which of these was a procedure required?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the procedure for obtaining permission from the city to bring prisoners from the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness you've testified there were three shifts of 12 hours, so that whenever you finished a shift of 12 hours, you would be free for 24 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, that was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You've also testified that in that period, that you were not on duty, that you would go home because your house was nearby and you would stay there. Now, is it fair to say that some of the soldiers in the period that they were not on duty would stay at the base or would hang around at the base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. What I didn't see, I can't speak about on behalf of anyone else. I can just tell you what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Whenever you were at the base, did you never see any soldiers whom you know that they were in shifts, hang around at the base drinking coffee or whatever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: When one came to the base, one did so only when there were some intensified activities, some reports, alert situation, because it was risky. There could be shells falling, so the request was that there should be as few soldiers there as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: One last question: Your group leader, would he be, when you were on duty on your shift, would the group leader also be at the confrontation line or would he remain at the base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group leader had to be with us on the front line, because it is from him that we received orders. He would designate people to go to which bunker, to determine shifts, whether we would be on duty at the bunker or one, two or three hours, who would be resting, so there had to be with us all the time and it's only normal that they were with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness MM, for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of the room. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to tender, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we would like to tender these two maps, D2/37 and D2/38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No objections to the maps, and the Prosecution would like to tender Exhibit P14.20, which is photograph of the health centre from January, 1996. All the other exhibits which I used were either admitted or tendered already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par, any objections to that photo?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I do not wish to tire you but I would sincerely like to know the source of this photograph, and if we could have the complete stamp that appears in the top left-hand corner, could the Prosecutor tell us the source, who provided this photograph, and also the complete stamp that appears on the top left-hand corner because in January, 1996, the Cyrillic script was certainly not used in the Bosniak-Croatian entity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bos, would you please provide some information for us about this stamp as well as this photo?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: This photograph is from a photo album, which was provided to us by the AID Mostar, and the photograph -- it was it's a series of photographs which according to the album were taken in January, 1996. That's all I can say on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since this document has been used extensively during the cross-examination and the re-examination, and there is no objections from Mr. Par, we decided this document is admitted into the evidence. It's so decided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Shall we have a break now and then we will have the next witness after the break. I have been reminded that the document D2/37 is under seal. We will resume at ten minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before we start, for the sake of the record, I have to say that D2/37 and D2/38 are both admitted into the evidence. Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please stand up? And make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, the usher will show you a piece of paper with your name on it. Please don't read it out. First just tell us whether that is indeed your name by saying yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Try to follow me in such a way that when I finish my question, make a brief pause and then start answering it, so that the interpreters can keep track of what we are saying. As I will be asking for some personal particulars, Mr. President, may we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: So because you were granted a pseudonym, I'll either use your pseudonym or as witness. So now, my question is, during the attack of the Serb aggression and the Yugoslav People's Army on Mostar, were you active militarily?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What unit did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: In the beginning it was before the unit was formed, when we became active and we joined, and later on I was with the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And you were with this unit until when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Until the 9th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what happened to you that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: We were captured by the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you describe it in some detail? What happened? Where were you? What were you doing? How far did you get before you were captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: We were on the front line facing the Serb aggressor, and on our way back home, that is when our shift was over, we were then captured by members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know which was the unit that captured you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. They were some, what you call it, some were masked, I mean they had paints, black paint over their faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what did they tell you? When did that exactly happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: It could have been in the early afternoon. They didn't say anything to us. They simply forced us into a vehicle and took us to the SDK building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And until that time, what were the relations between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croat Defence Council? What is your experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: One could sense the tension in the air. One could feel that not everything was all right but prior to that, there were those conflicts in Central Bosnia and it was then that one could feel tension in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And how many of you were captured that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, about nine of us, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And how long were you in captivity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: 18 days, until the 27th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: In the SDK building. It's something like the state bank, the building of the state bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what did the room that you were put in look like? How large was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, it was about four times four metres, 16 metres square, and we were about 40 there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You said that you were nine soldiers and altogether 40 persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes, about forty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Please wait for the question. Who else was there with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: There were civilians but there were also members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Who were the civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: The civilians were people who lived on that side and there were some also civilians who had been moving along this demarcation line and they were simply rounded up, picked up by vehicles of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what was the nationality of those civilians who had been captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Was there another prison in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: At that time I had no way of knowing but later on when I left, I heard that there was one in the fourth elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, people talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Of those persons who were detained with you, did you find anyone already there when you came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were a father and a son. I think about four or five people were there already when we arrived on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you find out when they had been captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: I think it was a day or two earlier, so it could have been on the 7th or 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you find out why they had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: There was no other reason but their Croat origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And before that, I mean before the 9th of May, 1993, did you see anything out of the order, anything unusual that might be -- that might indicate that a possible conflict between the BH Army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: When I went to the front line, and I believe it was the 7th of May, and as we climbed up Podvelezje I saw members of the BH Army dig some trenches, but then I didn't pay much attention but I did notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what were the conditions during your detention, I mean accommodation, food, treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, we were 40, as I've said, so it was crowded and I don't think there were two beds altogether so that we had to sleep on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And, well, was there any mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, it was still all fresh, how shall I put it, it was a fresh conflict. There was however one incident but there were some attempts, there were some attempts by those members of the BH Army to enter the prison, but the administrator would not let them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And then how and when were you released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: We were released on the 27th of May, through the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Was there the exchange?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes. We were exchanged on the 27th of May, with the mediation of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was the principle that governed the exchange? Just wait until my question. Was it one for one or all for all or what? Now you can answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: So you have to wait for me to finish my question and then a couple of seconds more.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: So where were you taken? Where was it that you were released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: We were released in front of the hospital at Bijeli Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And how were you brought there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: We were brought in buses, I think there were two to perhaps three buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And how many people were taken there altogether, to that particular place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, I know about us who were soldiers, about the rest I don't remember. About 40. 40 odd. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what happened to you after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: After that, I didn't join any unit. Well naturally I'd been captured, so I took some rest, and then later on, if I remember, in the beginning of June, I joined Stela's unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Why that unit precisely? Did you know Stela already?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Stela and I have been friends since we were children, and this unit, the 4th Battalion, I didn't like it any more, and I simply felt that my place was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And when did that happen? Do you know roughly when was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, say, for instance, could have been 10th June, 12th of June, sometime before the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And had that unit, Vinko Martinovic's unit, already taken shape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, it was at its embryonic stage, as the saying goes, in the -- there were some private donations and it was finally formed in -- within 20 days after that or so. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know which part of the Bulevar or the separation line was held by your unit? And if you do, can you point at it on this map of the town? Just make a circle and put the next number, whichever. I think it's number 4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No, it's number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, 3?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could we go to private session, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The photograph will be D2/40.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Look at the photograph, Witness, and tell us, if you can, show us and mark with a marker that section of the Bulevar, that segment, that section of the separation line, which was held by your unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have it on the ELMO? Do you know which were the units next to you, to the left and to the right of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: To the right of us was Benko Penavic, and to the left, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When you look at the photograph, like this, what is left, what is right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: When I look at it like this, to the left is the Benko Penavic unit, and to the right, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And where was the demarcation line of areas of responsibility that was under your unit and Benko Penavic's unit? Can you tell us where that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: That was on Liska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What was your unit's duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Our duty was to guard the front lines which had already been fortified.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What does that mean, fortified lines, in relation to this photograph and this number that you put on this building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: It means that the front line was fortified with, say, sand bags or were there were doors, there were also nailed and covered with more sand bags, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you ever leave the line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you ever -- were you ever assigned any other tasks apart from guarding the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No other tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how strong was the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: About 40, 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know who were then -- how they joined the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Those were mostly lads -- well, it was spontaneous. Those were mostly lads from, I don't know, from those areas, from those neighbourhoods, where I and Stela lived, and acquaintances and friends and like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And who was your commander, your unit's commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Stela.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what was his rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: There were no ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was Vinko Martinovic's deputy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: There were no deputies. It was spontaneous, and if somebody was appointed to lead a shift, but those shifts were not even permanent thing, and it was all simply spontaneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What did shift leaders do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Shift leaders led soldiers to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know who issued orders to Vinko Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Our unit was under the command of the town defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see or hear anyone issue either oral or written orders to Vinko Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know which larger unit did your unit, your Vinko Skrobo unit, belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: We were an independent unit, that is under the command of the defence of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you have your barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Then where did soldiers go after their shift on the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: The soldiers went home or, I don't know if those who had girl friends, they would go somewhere. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How -- what was the -- how long did shifts take?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Every shift was 12 hours long.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And now, when you were on duty, I'm talking about you, what were your tasks, how were you deployed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, there were no tasks to really write home about. Very simple. You just had to guard the line. For instance, I would be on the position at, as we called it hole, Rupa, I spent two hours there and then another soldier would come to take over and we would take some rest, have coffee and it was like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Now you tell us we were at the hole. What did you do there exactly? Did you just sit there looking through the sites or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what did it look like to you? Was it wearing could you manage it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, yes, one could manage it but it wasn't easy, it wasn't easy at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: But who then assigned you to those mini shifts, those mini two hour shifts within those 12 hours shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: I'm telling you it was all spontaneous. We got along well and we just talked it out between ourselves. It was nothing much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what about those soldiers on your shift who were not at the hole, as you put it? Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 14585 to 14593.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what did soldiers who were on the same shift but who were not at the hole?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, there were others, some were in the rear or were drinking coffee or resting and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Could you show on this photograph where that was? Just point at it, just point at it. You can leave the photograph on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, the soldiers were behind, behind this, in this building here, in the rear, and here is where were those holes, as we called them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You said part, you said something about sand bags. Was it the only kind that you used as a fortification for those openings? How were you fortified in this building, in the health centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, there were -- there was a door, I can't remember exactly, and it was boarded up, and over it there were sand bags.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Now, this building on the photograph that we see here, does it look the way it looked in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say so. The door was here, several doors, I think, and now they seem to be gone, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were there any barriers in the -- or across the Liska Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes, there were so-called hedgehogs, these are anti-tank barriers. I don't really know but say somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were there any obstacles put up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: In this area, only over there, back here, there were sand bags here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you then take the marker, I don't know which one we can see best, perhaps the red one, and put a -- many small circles in a string to indicate the location of these sandbags?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I see it. Where did you say you had those anti-tank obstacles make a series of small Xs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were there any other obstacles, barriers, visual ones?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: The sand bags, above the sandbags, there was a rope, a cord, on which carpets were hung.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: So can you then draw a line to show where this cord was stretched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of all this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, the purpose was to fortify it, it was a fortified front line those carpets that were hung there allowed us to move freely, otherwise they would have seen us and fired at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Was there daily fighting at the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't much of a fighting, it was as -- it was sporadic gun fire, as it is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you hear, either from stories or you personally, who held the front line on the opposite side, that is on the side held by the Bosnia-Herzegovina Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: You mean which unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes, which unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you ever communicate with them, talk with them, call out to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes. There were such occurrences.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Why, when, on what occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, simply perhaps one knew somebody over there so they talked, sometimes people crossed over on their own from the west bank to the left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you point on this photograph where were those soldiers to whom you called or who called out to you? Leave it there and use the pointer, use the pointer to point out, it not on the monitor. On the ELMO. You have to do it on the ELMO but don't remove the photograph. Yes, like this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: [indicates] Yes, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you describe to us this building, what it looks like now for the record, what is it now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: You mean this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, if I remember it --

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. What is there now, what can you see there now? What do you see there now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: I see this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what does it look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: You mean now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes, now, what you see.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, I think the same, I don't remember. I mean is it in ruins or does it have a roof?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No, it doesn't have a roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Oh, it doesn't have a roof?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No, I don't see it, what it looks like on the photographer, it doesn't have a roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did your unit have any duties to perform in town to persecute Muslims, to evict them from homes, to stop them, to ask them for IDs to arrest them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: We were a unit that secured the fortified lines at the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did your unit and you personally take part in any way in the eviction of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: I personally did not and I'm not aware of any cases of others doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of cases of crossovers by Muslims across the line in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: You mean voluntary crossovers? Yes, I am aware of that. For instance, in some cases, a mother may have had a son there and she wanted to pass and she was allowed to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You personally -- did you personally have this experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes. I had this case when this acquaintance of mine, who had a son on the other side, asked me to let her cross, and I did so. She packed two or three suitcases. I even helped her to carry those suitcases to the front line. I called out that fire should be ceased. We called over to the other side, telling them,"Your people are coming over." And she crossed without any difficulties or problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of any rumours that Stela and the Stelici, his soldiers, as they were called, took part in the persecution of Muslims in looting and the like? Did you hear any such rumours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear such rumours, later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you check them out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: I personally have no authority to be able to check them out myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you see Vinko Martinovic's reaction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: I just know that he was angry. I know it's normal, that he couldn't be indifferent, as he was -- he had authority, someone used or abused that authority for some negative purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were prisoners brought to your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Maybe ten or 15 prisoners would be brought over from the Heliodrom to do some light labour. There were four or five mechanics that repaired private vehicles, the ambulances and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Was this on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: The mechanics were there frequently. As for the others, they came when needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What did they do in connection with the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: They repaired private passenger cars, the work of an auto mechanic. On one occasion, I think they repaired ambulances, two or three times, then they also adjusted vehicles that went to the confrontation line. They armoured them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did the prisoners sleep at the unit's base or headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Sometimes they did. There was a small group that slept there. They were mostly acquaintances, who I believe felt safer if they slept there, but that wasn't always the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how sleeping was organised, where they slept? Did they have bed linens, beds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes, they had normal conditions like everyone else, like the men on duty, who, -- among the soldiers who slept there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did anyone guard them with weapons? Were there they under any kind of threat, under guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No, there was simply no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: As far as you can remember, can you describe the conditions for them, food, water, was it sufficient, were they mistreated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: As I was saying, they were mostly guys from the town that were well known, and then their wives might come. We would give them everything we had. So we shared everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, was any one of them wounded or killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you do -- did they do any hard labour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: These were all light duties. There was no need for any hard labour, cleaning for instance, of the surrounding area and the mechanics that I mentioned, so all these things were easy jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did they have any compensation for what they did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: For instance, if somebody repaired somebody's car, then the owner would give him cigarettes, food and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what you yourself saw, how did Vinko Martinovic treat them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were they taken to do work at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did they work on the Bulevar itself, in front of the health centre building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were there any trenches in front of the health centre building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No trenches, not at all, out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of a person by the name of Nenad Harmandic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. He was known as a "genter" in town, in other words an agent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see him come to your unit, among the prisoners that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Halil Ajanic, known as Lopata?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes. I've heard of him. He was a city joker, a drunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about his stay with the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge, or have you heard, of the incident in which his son was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes. I heard of the incident. His son was on good terms with a German man, I can't remember his name. He was the mascot of that German, he went with him everywhere, to his apartment, the apartment that the German lived in, and as he kept his weapons and grenades inside, the boy, as far as I heard, picked up a hand grenade like any child, he caught the fuse and the bomb went off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know or have you heard that he considers Vinko Martinovic to be responsible for that event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: I heard that only the other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the 17th of September, 1993? Were you on the front line on that date? There was a major conflict on that day between the BH Army and the HVO, and a tank was used on that day. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: On that day, there was a coordinated operation, the aim being to break through the lines of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know along which route the tank moved? Could you show us that on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: So the tank was behind the sandbags, the sandbags, here therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And did it fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: I think it fired two or three shells. Then there was a lull.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Could you mark with a letter "T" exactly where the tank was when it fired, on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did the tank move in front of the sandbags at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Could it have passed, if it wanted to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: It couldn't pass because of the sandbags, the sandbags were a barrier, an obstacle. Now, whether it could actually pass, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you see the prisoners on that day there, thereabouts where the tank was moving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you hear or see in the media, in the press, what Vinko Martinovic is being charged with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: I don't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Prosecution claims that the prisoners were in uniform, that they were armed with wooden rifles, and that they were used as a human shield for the tank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes, I know that that is the allegation of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: I can say that that is not the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of a story to that effect, that is wooden rifles being used, somewhere else in battle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: I heard later on stories that these soldiers with wooden rifles were seen somewhere in Central Bosnia or something like that, but I really don't know. Believe me. These are just rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with that part of the indictment that Stela and Stelicis are charged that is your whole unit, for expulsion and looting of Muslim families and their eviction to the eastern parts of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you receive a salary while you were a soldier in the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How and who paid you that salary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: I don't know who paid us but I know the logistics man went to Grude and brought us our salaries in cash.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And where did you physically pick up the money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: At the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That ends my examination-in-chief, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, cross-examination, Mr. Scott. I'm sorry to interrupt you, we will stop at ten minutes past.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I know you've told us that after you were released from being held by the ABiH, you joined Vinko Martinovic, Stela's unit. I'd like to ask you a few more questions about that. Can you tell us exactly how it was that you joined the unit? I mean how did you actually go about that? Did you just -- did you know where the headquarters was located it at the time and just walked through the front door and said, "I'm joining the unit" or how did you actually join the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: There was no big secret about that. As Stela and I knew one another it was very simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, tell us. I mean as much as you can recall and I know it's sometime ago, but just describe to us how you joined the unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, exactly in the way I said. It was so simple that you won't believe me. I simply saw Stela, I said that I'd like to join his unit, as he knew me, he knew what kind of a person I was, he trusted me, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Prior to the time that you were held by the ABiH, you were a member of an HVO unit, were you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes, it was the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who was your immediate commanding officer at the time in early, let's say in early May, 1993, before you were held on the 9th of May, who was your commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't remember. They changed a lot. So it's hard to recollect now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, when you were released from being held and you decided to join Stela's unit, did you go to your prior commander and say something to him, "Oh, by the way I've decided to leave your unit, I don't like it any more and I'm going to do down the street and join another HVO unit organised by Stela"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: As Stela knew these members of the 4th Battalion, then, upon his suggestion, they allowed me to transfer to his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, how do you know that? How do you know, if it happened at all, how do you know that Stela supposedly went to someone in authority in your prior unit, in the 4th Battalion and obtained permission essentially for a transfer, you were transferred from one HVO unit to another unit. So how do you know that Stela did anything to arrange that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: How I know? Simply because Stela told me. It was simply something legal. It was up to me if I don't like it in one unit any more, it was up to me to simply join which unit I wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So it's your testimony to the Judges, sir, that members of the HVO, military soldiers, had the ability in the HVO to move from unit to unit at will?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: I didn't say that quite like that but since my case was a specific one, as I had been captured, simply I didn't feel -- I didn't feel like a member of that unit. It was a psychological trauma, that was linked to this 4th Battalion and I didn't want to have anything more to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, did you turn in your equipment, for instance, did you still have a weapon at that time? Did you have a small arm, an automatic rifle, that had been issued to you by the prior unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: I returned them to them with satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When did you return these items to your prior unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm sorry, no, I didn't return them, because our weapons were seized from us when we were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that your transfer to the Vinko Martinovic unit, as far as you know, was nothing more than you going to Mr. Martinovic, according to you, and just saying you wanted to join his unit, and beyond that, you have no knowledge, do you, of how that was actually carried out, or if in fact anything was done, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Nothing in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you ever an officer or did you have any command responsibilities in the Vinko Skrobo unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No. I was an ordinary soldier, a private.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the Vinko Skrobo unit, sir, did you ever issue an order to anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: As I was a foot soldier, how could I issue orders to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the headquarters which you've located on the map, did Stela have a particular office, that is his own office, in the headquarters building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: It was his office, and everybody's. It wasn't any special office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that in this building from the basement to the top floor, in no part of that building was there any particular office that belonged to the commander, that was the commander's office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: There was a table where Stela sat, a table and chair, but no separate room or special room. Soldiers would come there and sit there. It was a collective room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where in the building, as best you can recall, help us, please, where in the building was this table and chair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: On this photograph, you can't see that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I know. I understand. I'm not asking to you look at a photograph right now. Just physically describe, was it on the ground floor as you walked in the build, as you walked in the front door did you turn to the right and go into a room, or was it on the next floor up or was it in the basement, just tell us where was this table and chair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: You entered, so it was in the ground floor, when you enter, let me try and remember, you enter like this, and then to the right, yes, let's see, this was that room, so I enter this way, this is the door, and the table was over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you did have to go through another interior door into a some other room and the table and chair was in that room, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: There was the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we object to these questions. If there is any dispute as to this person being a member of the Vinko Skrobo unit, the Prosecution seems to be challenging that. If he's not challenging it, then I don't know what the aim of these questions are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, frankly speaking, Mr. Scott, we really don't know where you are going to lead us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do have a goal in -- a very specific goal in mind. I'm not challenging the witness's membership in the unit. I just thought among other things after all these months it might be interesting to know, and since by all accounts prisoners were going in and out of the building and people were going in and out of the building on a daily basis just exactly where it was Stela was located. And so I think I should be allowed to ask at least a couple more questions about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may pursue it to this direction but frankly speaking, we don't think it is very important for us to know where Mr. Martinovic sat at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Mr. President, I'll keep it limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the last question I put to you before the objection was, so it was the case that as you came in through the main entrance, you went through a -- another interior door. You understand what I mean. Into a room where this table and chair were located.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: When you go through the entrance of this building, there is a kind of corridor and then the door of this room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, were you ever in this room, sir, when, for instance, Stela was meeting with any of the group commanders or any of the shift commanders or people that he was exercising military authority over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: We happened to be there in company, we would be talking, having coffee, and I was never present at any kind of a meeting or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the next question, please listen, it's a little different than the one I just asked you: Did you ever attend any meetings that Stela participated in with his commanders, that is the commander or commanders above him? Did you ever attend any such meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So sir, if I understand your testimony, you never participated in any meeting with Stela and his subordinate commanders, and likewise, you never participated in a meeting between Stela and his commanders, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: As I was saying, I was a foot soldier. If there were any such meetings, I have no idea about them. I was just an ordinary soldier and there was no need for me to go there. What would I be doing at those meetings, if there were any meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll accept what you say to this extent. If there were such meetings, as you say if there were such meetings your answer to my question then is no, you were never involved in any such meetings, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Loud and clear, I was never at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, did these different groups, if there was something called -- I want to make it clear I'm not indicating these are technical names or titles that might have been used but in a functional sense, if there were these groups or group commanders or shift commanders, did a group or a shift have any name? Did you have a subunit name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you weren't the third platoon or the Vinko Skrobo/2 or the third shift? You had no reference point or name that your group would use; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Probably there was something like numbers, one, two, three, but just now I don't remember, but there must have been something to distinguish among the shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I'm not sure now if you said this or not, to be honest so I'll just ask you again, who was your group leader then or shift commander whichever term you're more comfortable with, who was the commander or leader of your group or shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: You mean the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Ernest Takac was my shift leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I believe you testified, sir, on direct examination, that throughout 1993, your continuous assignment, your duty station, as it were, was the confrontation line and a location inside the building called the health centre; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I heard you correctly, and I didn't -- not sure I followed it, my apology -- during your testimony, you said there was something called the hole. Was this -- this was a location that was located toward the back -- using -- saying the confrontation line was the front side, if you will, the front of the building, the hole was something located a spot located in the back part of the health centre building? Is that what you told us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: May I show it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, please show us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, holes were, say, there were two or three or, I don't know how many, on this side, facing -- facing the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I may have misunderstood, sir. I thought the holes were some place that you went when you were not immediately manning your station but you had a bit of a break during this 12 hour shift you would go to one of the holes. Did I misunderstand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No, you misunderstood me. That is our local name for the openings for rifles, so these are openings through which you push your rifle and then fire if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. During a 12 hour shift, then, were you at these holes then, as you just clarified were you at the hole for the full 12 hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, because it was very hard on us, a soldier would spend, say, about two hours, and then another one would come and take over, and this one would go to the rear, to another building, to get some rest, have a coffee, have a fag.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you show us on the photograph that we have been using, when you say you would go to an area, the soldier would go to an area in the rear, can you see that on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: This building here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So based on what you've told us in the last moment or two, during a regular 12 hour shift, how much of that shift would you actually be manning your position or hole?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, let's see, if we were some 15 soldiers, then it means that not all the soldiers attended to those holes, but it was only an agreement. It was all spontaneous. There was no firm -- firm agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, no one is going to -- I don't think anyone will expect you to speak with complete precision on this but again I'm sure it varied sometimes from day to day but on average during a normal 12 hour shift, and if you're reluctant to say, let me suggest and you can disagree with me, would it be fair to say that on a normal 12 hour shift you might actually be at your position for, say, four hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Well, about two hours, but these were not the only holes. There were other -- as we look at it now, there were some to the right, where the positions were too. So that it wasn't -- I mean it would be stupidly literal that you have one building and you can see only in front of you, only ahead of you. It is I think normal that you are able to look both to your left and to your right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So in a particular 12 hour shift you might take a position at more than one hole. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: No, no. For instance, let's say there could be perhaps indicators of the positions, 1, 2, 3 and there be five soldiers at position 1, five at position 2, five at position 3, and while those five soldiers at a position could spend there two hours or I don't really know what does it come up to, I can't calculate it right now, but it was spontaneous, it was amongst ourselves, about two hours, you can say that we spent there about two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So we can understand then, sir, that in a formal 12 -- you had a 12 hour shift and then it was it clear that you were then off for 24 hours before your next shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During any particular 36 hour period, sir, you actually manned a position for about two hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: Right. That is perhaps too rigid. At sometimes it was three hours, at sometimes it was four hours but then somebody might be tired and we can't really -- it's difficult for me to define it. Those were spontaneous. Those were spontaneous watches.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, the shift you were on, was it always the same shift or did the shift change from time to time? Was it during the night-time -- did part of your shift -- and one day were you on night and the next day or 24 hours later you were on days, or how did that work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
utterances.text: I didn't quite get your meaning. What were you driving at?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you on the same shift for an extended period of time? For instance and you can tell us, what was your normal starting time, let's say the summer of 1993, you just worked a 12 hour shift, did you start at 12.00 noon and work until 12 clock midnight, or what was your shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MN
